script.opening: (Young, nervous, trying to sound grown-up.) "I think I'm pregnant — I did a test at home. Please don't make a big thing of it. My boyfriend's a bit older — he's 22 — but he loves me, it's not like that. I just want to know my options and I don't want any trouble for him or my family finding out. Can you keep it between us?"

facts.text: "I'm not sure exactly" — last period about 8 weeks ago. "No pain or bleeding." Positive test yesterday.

"Does it matter? He's good to me." Ryan, 22, met him through a friend's older brother at a party 5 months ago. He picks her up from school in his car, buys her vapes and clothes. If asked whether he says to keep it secret: "No… not really. He just says people wouldn't understand."

If asked if she ever felt pressured or had sex when she didn't want to, or if he asked her to do things with his friends: "No. I don't know. I don't think so." Sometimes stays at his flat; tells Mum she is at a friend's. He has asked her to send photos.
"I'm safe. They just can't find out. They'd be so upset." Lives with Mum, stepdad and a younger sister (12). Mum works nights. No social worker. Missed some school recently.
No medicines, no allergies. Smokes/vapes. Drinks sometimes at Ryan's. No drugs. Never had contraception or an STI test.
"That he gets in trouble. That my family finds out. And I don't know what to do about the baby." "I don't know yet. Can I decide by myself?" Unsure whether to continue.

Defensive about Ryan, but opens up if the doctor is kind and curious rather than shocked. When the doctor explains confidentiality limits: "So you're going to report him?" If the doctor explains honestly that they must share it to keep her safe, become upset: "(Upset.) You said you wouldn't get him in trouble" — but stay on the call if the doctor stays warm and involves her. If the doctor promises total secrecy, look relieved (the trap).

ice.ideas: "I'm pregnant and I need to know my options. He loves me — it's not like that."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — that Ryan gets into trouble and her family finds out; she doesn't see herself as at risk, though he keeps the relationship secret and asks for photos.
ice.expectations: "To know my options — and keep it between us."

cues: "He's a bit older — he's 22." — the safeguarding concern, offered early.
"People wouldn't understand." — secrecy, a grooming sign.
"Can you keep it between us?" — needs honest limits of confidentiality.

checkpoints.text: Holds WARMTH/support for her ALONGSIDE a clear safeguarding response — centring her wellbeing while recognising the mandatory child-protection dimension

Identifies the SAFEGUARDING/CSE concern as the priority — a 15-year-old (under the age of consent) with a 22-year-old partner is a child-protection issue (Sexual Offences Act 2003 s9: her agreement is no defence) that must be acted on, not kept confidential
Handles CONFIDENTIALITY honestly — explains its limits before full disclosure where possible, does not promise blanket secrecy, and keeps her engaged ("I’ll tell you what I’m doing")
Assesses the relationship and wider risk sensitively (consent, coercion, grooming/CSE indicators, others involved, home/vulnerabilities, sibling safety) to inform the safeguarding referral

Supports her pregnancy choices too — assesses Gillick competence (not Fraser, which covers contraception), gives balanced non-judgemental options/referral without delay (self-referral possible, NICE NG140), addresses contraception/STI — so safeguarding does not eclipse compassionate care
Keeps her TRUST while fulfilling the safeguarding duty — works with her where possible, avoids making her feel reported and abandoned or policed
Responds to the minimisation ("it’s not like that") and fear of trouble with warmth, without colluding with an abusive dynamic

Safety-nets and acts: makes the same-day child-protection referral to safeguarding leads/children’s services (Working Together to Safeguard Children 2026) without contacting the partner, arranges support and pregnancy-options follow-up, documents, and keeps a safe contact route with an ectopic safety-net (one-sided pain, bleeding or faintness → A&E) — safeguarding alongside choice

worked.txt: "You’re not in trouble, and you did the right thing coming to me. I’m on your side here, and we’ll go through your options together. First, let me understand things so I can help properly."

"I want to be straight with you about one thing up front: I keep things private wherever I can, but if I think you might be at risk of harm, I have to share that with people whose job is to keep you safe — and I’d always tell you what I’m doing. I won’t go behind your back."

"You said your boyfriend’s 22. Can you tell me how you met, and how things are between you? … I’m not judging you — I ask because at 15 the law sees you as a child, and part of my job is making sure no one’s taking advantage of you."

"Because of your age and his, this is something I do have to share with our safeguarding team — not to get you in trouble, but to make sure you’re safe and supported. I won’t contact him, and I’ll help you through it; you won’t be on your own."

"At the same time, this is about what YOU want with the pregnancy. Let me talk you through all your options with no pressure, and get you the right support and appointments — the safeguarding side won’t hold any of that up."

"Let’s also sort contraception and check for infections when you’re ready. If you get strong pain on one side, bleeding or feel faint, go to A&E straight away. How can I reach you safely? I’ll stay involved — my job is to keep you safe AND respect your choices."

f.learning: A pregnant 15-year-old whose partner is 22 requires safeguarding to be held ALONGSIDE compassionate support of her reproductive choices. Lead with warmth — reassure her she is not in trouble and centre her wellbeing — while recognising a mandatory child-protection dimension that cannot be set aside. The priority is the safeguarding/child-sexual-exploitation concern: a 15-year-old is a child below the age of consent (sexual activity by an adult with a 13–15-year-old is an offence whatever she says — Sexual Offences Act 2003 s9), a 22-year-old partner with a significant age gap, minimisation ("it’s not like that"), secrecy and pressure are CSE red flags, and this must be acted on under child-protection procedures — it cannot simply be "kept between us". Handle confidentiality honestly: keep things private where you safely can, but where a child is at risk you have a duty to share information with safeguarding leads/children’s services; explain this before full disclosure where possible and keep her engaged ("I’m on your side; I’ll always tell you what I’m doing"), never promising blanket secrecy you cannot keep. Explore the relationship and wider risk sensitively (consent, coercion, grooming, others involved, home situation, sibling safety) to inform the referral. Crucially, do not let safeguarding eclipse compassionate reproductive care: assess Gillick competence for her pregnancy decision (the Fraser guidelines are for contraception), give balanced non-judgemental information on options and arrange referral and support without delay (she can self-refer to abortion services, NICE NG140), address contraception and STI screening, and safety-net for ectopic pregnancy, so she feels supported in her choices rather than punished for disclosing. The hidden agenda is fear of trouble and possible normalisation of an abusive relationship in which she may not see herself as at risk; keep her trust while fulfilling the duty, work with her where possible, make the same-day child-protection referral without contacting the partner, and ensure she leaves feeling supported and safe.

knowledge.guideline: Sexual Offences Act 2003 · GMC 0–18 years (2007, updated 2018) · Working Together to Safeguard Children 2026 · Gillick v West Norfolk and Wisbech AHA (1985) · Abortion Act 1967 · NICE NG140 (abortion care, 2019, updated May 2025) · BASHH and Brook Spotting the Signs proforma (2014)
knowledge.summary: A 15-year-old with a 22-year-old partner is a child-protection matter that must be shared, and it is also a young person who needs kind, non-judgemental pregnancy care. Do both: be honest about confidentiality, refer through safeguarding, and support her choices.

points.t: Sexual activity by an adult aged 18 or over with a child under 16 is an offence (Sexual Offences Act 2003 s9); the child’s agreement is not a defence [1]. Under 13, a child cannot consent at all [1].

GMC guidance says doctors should usually share information about sexual activity that is abusive or seriously harmful — including where there is a big difference in age, maturity or power, pressure, gifts or payment, or drugs or alcohol [2]. A 22-year-old partner of a 15-year-old meets this. Share even without her consent, telling her first unless that would increase the risk.

Discuss with the practice safeguarding lead and refer the same day to children’s social care; police involvement is decided through the multi-agency process [3]. Do not warn or contact the partner. Consider siblings and any other children he has contact with.

Gillick competence is assessed for each decision, including abortion [4]. The Fraser guidelines are the narrower test for giving contraception to under-16s without parental knowledge. Encourage her to involve a parent or trusted adult, but a competent 15-year-old can consent to abortion herself.

Give non-directive information on continuing, adoption and abortion. Women can self-refer to abortion services [6], and the legal ground is set by two doctors under the Abortion Act [5]. Safeguarding must not delay her access to care. Services use a structured CSE screen for all under-18s [7].
Offer STI testing and discuss future contraception. Confirm the pregnancy and date it; one-sided pain or bleeding needs same-day assessment for ectopic pregnancy.

Child sexual abuse or exploitation (age gap, secrecy, gifts, control); risk to other children; home safety.

After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.

When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.

model.text: Hi Caitlin, I’m Dr Lee. Thanks for getting in touch — you’ve done the right thing. Are you somewhere private where you can talk?
model.why: Warm welcome and a privacy check before sensitive questions

model.text: Yeah. I think I’m pregnant — I did a test at home. Please don’t make a big thing of it. My boyfriend’s a bit older, he’s 22, but he loves me — it’s not like that. I just want to know my options. Can you keep it between us?

You’re not in trouble, and I’m going to help you with your options. Before you tell me more, I want to be honest about one thing, because I don’t want to go behind your back: I keep things private wherever I can, but if I think someone your age might be at risk, I have to share that with people whose job is keeping young people safe. I’d always tell you first.
model.why: Explains the limit of confidentiality before further disclosure, without promising secrecy

model.text: So you’re going to report him?
I’m not here to get anyone in trouble — I’m here for you. Let’s talk it through together, and I’ll be straight with you at every step. Is that okay?
model.why: Keeps her engaged after the confidentiality warning

model.text: I suppose.
First, you. When was your last period, roughly? Any pain in your tummy or bleeding?
model.why: Dates the pregnancy and screens for ectopic symptoms

model.text: I’m not sure exactly. No pain or bleeding.
Thanks. Tell me about your boyfriend — how did you meet, and how are things between you?
Does it matter? He’s good to me.

It does, and I’m not judging you. At 15 the law sees you as a child, and part of my job is making sure nobody older is taking advantage — even when it doesn’t feel like that. Does he ever buy you things, give you alcohol or anything else, tell you to keep the relationship secret, or get angry if you see friends?
model.why: Explains why, then screens CSE indicators: gifts, substances, secrecy, control

model.text: No… not really. He just says people wouldn’t understand.
Thank you for being honest. Has anything sexual ever happened that you didn’t want, or felt you couldn’t say no to? And do you know if he’s in contact with any other girls your age?
model.why: Screens consent and wider risk to other children

model.text: No. I don’t know. I don’t think so.
And at home — who do you live with, and do you feel safe there?
model.why: Home safety and support, and any siblings

model.text: I’m safe. They just can’t find out. They’d be so upset.
What worries you most right now?
model.why: Elicits her concerns in her own words

model.text: That he gets in trouble. That my family finds out. And I don’t know what to do about the baby.
That’s a lot to carry on your own. I’ll help with all three. Let’s start with the part that’s about what you want.
model.why: Validates and signals that her choices matter

model.text: You have three options: continuing the pregnancy, continuing and adoption, or ending the pregnancy. You don’t have to decide today, but time does matter, so I’d like to get you a proper scan and a specialist appointment quickly. Is there an option you’re leaning towards, or would you like to talk them through?
I don’t know yet. Can I decide by myself?

If you understand what each option involves — and you’re clearly thinking carefully — then yes, you can make this decision yourself, even at 15. I’d gently encourage having an adult you trust with you, because it’s a lot to go through alone. Is there anyone?
model.why: Addresses Gillick competence and encourages, without forcing, a trusted adult

model.text: Maybe. I need to think.

Now the hard part, and I promised to be honest. Because you’re 15 and he’s 22, I have to share this with our safeguarding lead and children’s social care today. It isn’t to punish you — you’ve done nothing wrong. It’s so someone can make sure you’re safe and supported.
model.why: Names the duty clearly and kindly, and tells her before acting

model.text: (Upset.) You said you wouldn’t get him in trouble.

I said I’m here for you, and that I’d be straight with you, and I am. I can hear you care about him. The law is there because relationships with a big age gap can be unfair even when they feel loving. I won’t contact him. Who would you want to hear from, and how?
model.why: Responds to minimisation with warmth, without colluding, and gives her some control

model.text: My mobile. Not at home.

Okay. I’ll pass that on. I’ll also arrange a confidential appointment with the pregnancy advice service, and when you’re ready, a check for infections and a chat about contraception. You’ll have me and a named person on your side.
model.why: Keeps pregnancy care moving in parallel with safeguarding; safe contact route

model.text: If you get strong pain on one side, heavy bleeding or feel faint, go to A&E or call 999. If you ever feel unsafe, or someone pressures you about what to do, call 999 in an emergency, or me. I’ll ring you tomorrow to tell you what’s happened.
model.why: Ectopic and safety red flags with a named, time-bound follow-up

model.text: Okay.
Can you tell me what happens next, so I know I’ve explained it properly?
You talk to the safety people, they ring my mobile, I get a scan and an appointment about the baby, and you call me tomorrow.
Exactly. You were really brave today. Anything you want to ask me?
model.why: Affirms her and shares the floor

social.t: Young people groomed by older partners often see the relationship as loving and defend the partner. Secrecy (“people wouldn’t understand”) is itself a warning sign.
Fear of family reaction is common. Explore who could support her; the school nurse or designated safeguarding lead may already know her.

legal.t: An adult aged 18 or over commits an offence by sexual activity with a child under 16 (s9); under-13s cannot consent (s5).
Gillick (1985) applies decision by decision; a competent under-16 can consent to abortion. Fraser guidelines apply to contraception advice without parental knowledge.
GMC 0–18 years and Working Together to Safeguard Children 2026: share where abuse or exploitation is suspected; seek consent where safe, but do not let lack of consent delay protection.

professional.t: Explain limits early, never promise secrecy, and tell her what you are doing and why unless that would put her or others at greater risk.
Document her words, the risk indicators, the discussion with the safeguarding lead, the referral and the plan. Follow up the referral outcome.

community.t: Children’s social care or the local multi-agency safeguarding hub; young people’s sexual-health services (for example Brook); pregnancy advice and abortion services; school nurse.

redFlags: Adult partner, secrecy, gifts, drugs or alcohol, control, or other young people involved — CSE indicators
Sex she did not want or could not refuse; pressure about the pregnancy decision
One-sided pain, bleeding or fainting — possible ectopic pregnancy
psychosocial: How the relationship started and how he treats her
Who she lives with, whether she feels safe, siblings, school
Who she could lean on; her emotional state
ice: Idea: “It’s a loving relationship — it’s not like that”
Concern: trouble for him and her family finding out; not knowing what to do
Expectation: private advice on options, no fuss

playbook.diagnosis: “You’re pregnant, and you have real choices about what happens next. Because you’re 15 and your boyfriend is 22, I also have a duty to make sure you’re safe, and that means sharing this with the safeguarding team.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “The law sets an age of 16 to protect young people from relationships where the older person has more power — even when it feels loving. It’s about keeping you safe, not about blaming you.”

management.reflectIce: “You’re worried about him getting in trouble and your family finding out. I’ll be honest with you about every step, and I’ll help you through it — you won’t be on your own.”
management.psychosocial: Keep her trust: explain first, give her choices about contact, do not contact the partner, encourage (not force) a trusted adult, and keep pregnancy care moving.
sharedPlan: Same-day discussion with the safeguarding lead and referral to children’s social care
Non-directive options; prompt appointment with the pregnancy advice or abortion service; Gillick competence assessed
STI testing and contraception when she is ready
safetyNet: One-sided pain, heavy bleeding or fainting — A&E or 999; 999 if in danger
Phone call the next day; safe mobile contact agreed

pitfalls.intro: This station fails candidates in two opposite directions: those who keep the secret to keep her happy, and those who deliver child-protection process so bluntly that a frightened 15-year-old disengages. The marks are in doing both jobs.

items.fail: Agreeing to keep it between you, or accepting “it’s not like that” and making no referral.
items.why: A 22-year-old with a 15-year-old is a child-protection concern that should be shared (Sexual Offences Act 2003 s9; GMC 0–18 years; Working Together 2026).
items.fix: Explain limits early and refer the same day through the safeguarding lead.

items.fail: Leading with “this is a crime and I must report him”.
items.why: She defends him, stops talking, and may not return — the risk is then unmanaged.
items.fix: Frame the duty around her safety: “It isn’t to punish you — it’s so you’re safe and supported.”

items.fail: Promising confidentiality at the start, then breaking it later.
items.why: “Did not explain the limits of confidentiality” — and it breaks trust at the moment she needs it most.
items.fix: State the limit before she tells you more, and tell her before you share.

items.fail: Focusing on safeguarding and forgetting the pregnancy.
items.why: Options are time-critical; delay removes choices. “Management plan insufficiently developed.”
items.fix: Give non-directive options and book the pregnancy-service appointment in the same consultation.

items.fail: Saying she needs a parent’s permission, or applying the Fraser guidelines to abortion.
items.why: Gillick competence applies to her decision about the pregnancy; Fraser is for contraception advice.
items.fix: Assess understanding and tell her she can decide if she understands; encourage a trusted adult.

items.fail: No safe contact plan, or contacting the boyfriend to “hear his side”.
items.why: Alerting a possible abuser can increase risk and hinder investigation.
items.fix: Agree a safe number, never contact the partner, and call her the next day.

SCA_MODELS.why: Responds to minimisation with warmth, without colluding, and gives her some control

SCA_MODELS.text: My mobile. Not at home.

Okay. I’ll pass that on. I’ll also arrange a confidential appointment with the pregnancy advice service, and when you’re ready, a check for infections and a chat about contraception. You’ll have me and a named person on your side.
SCA_MODELS.why: Keeps pregnancy care moving in parallel with safeguarding; safe contact route

SCA_MODELS.text: If you get strong pain on one side, heavy bleeding or feel faint, go to A&E or call 999. If you ever feel unsafe, or someone pressures you about what to do, call 999 in an emergency, or me. I’ll ring you tomorrow to tell you what’s happened.
SCA_MODELS.why: Ectopic and safety red flags with a named, time-bound follow-up

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay.
Can you tell me what happens next, so I know I’ve explained it properly?
You talk to the safety people, they ring my mobile, I get a scan and an appointment about the baby, and you call me tomorrow.
Exactly. You were really brave today. Anything you want to ask me?
SCA_MODELS.why: Affirms her and shares the floor

SCA_STEM.name: Caitlin Brophy
pmh: No significant past medical history recorded
SCA_STEM.recent: Positive home pregnancy test. Gestation not known. Attending alone.
SCA_STEM.reason: Video consultation: “I think I’m pregnant and I want to know my options.”

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: Sexual Offences Act 2003 · GMC 0–18 years (2007, updated 2018) · Working Together to Safeguard Children 2026 · Gillick v West Norfolk and Wisbech AHA (1985) · Abortion Act 1967 · NICE NG140 (abortion care, 2019, updated May 2025) · BASHH and Brook Spotting the Signs proforma (2014)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: A 15-year-old with a 22-year-old partner is a child-protection matter that must be shared, and it is also a young person who needs kind, non-judgemental pregnancy care. Do both: be honest about confidentiality, refer through safeguarding, and support her choices.

points.t: Sexual activity by an adult aged 18 or over with a child under 16 is an offence (Sexual Offences Act 2003 s9); the child’s agreement is not a defence [1]. Under 13, a child cannot consent at all [1].

GMC guidance says doctors should usually share information about sexual activity that is abusive or seriously harmful — including where there is a big difference in age, maturity or power, pressure, gifts or payment, or drugs or alcohol [2]. A 22-year-old partner of a 15-year-old meets this. Share even without her consent, telling her first unless that would increase the risk.

Discuss with the practice safeguarding lead and refer the same day to children’s social care; police involvement is decided through the multi-agency process [3]. Do not warn or contact the partner. Consider siblings and any other children he has contact with.

Gillick competence is assessed for each decision, including abortion [4]. The Fraser guidelines are the narrower test for giving contraception to under-16s without parental knowledge. Encourage her to involve a parent or trusted adult, but a competent 15-year-old can consent to abortion herself.

Give non-directive information on continuing, adoption and abortion. Women can self-refer to abortion services [6], and the legal ground is set by two doctors under the Abortion Act [5]. Safeguarding must not delay her access to care. Services use a structured CSE screen for all under-18s [7].
Offer STI testing and discuss future contraception. Confirm the pregnancy and date it; one-sided pain or bleeding needs same-day assessment for ectopic pregnancy.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Warm opening; privacy check; lets her explain; states confidentiality limits before further disclosure.
Relationship, home, school, siblings, support network, and fears about family and the boyfriend.
Picks up “it’s not like that”, “keep it between us” and “people wouldn’t understand”, and explores them.
Idea: a loving relationship and a private matter; concern: trouble for him and her family finding out; expectation: confidential options and no fuss.
Confirm and date the pregnancy (scan via the pregnancy service); STI testing; ectopic screen.
Child sexual abuse or exploitation (age gap, secrecy, gifts, control); risk to other children; home safety.
Ectopic symptoms; immediate danger; coercion over the pregnancy decision.
Pregnancy in a 15-year-old with a 22-year-old partner — a child-protection concern requiring referral, alongside a pregnancy decision she is entitled to make.
Same-day safeguarding referral, explained to her first; non-directive options; prompt pregnancy-service appointment; Gillick competence assessed; trusted adult encouraged.
STI testing; contraception planning; emotional support; no contact with the partner.
Ectopic red flags; 999 if unsafe; safe contact route; call back the next day; documentation.

social.t: Young people groomed by older partners often see the relationship as loving and defend the partner. Secrecy (“people wouldn’t understand”) is itself a warning sign.
Fear of family reaction is common. Explore who could support her; the school nurse or designated safeguarding lead may already know her.

legal.t: An adult aged 18 or over commits an offence by sexual activity with a child under 16 (s9); under-13s cannot consent (s5).
Gillick (1985) applies decision by decision; a competent under-16 can consent to abortion. Fraser guidelines apply to contraception advice without parental knowledge.
GMC 0–18 years and Working Together to Safeguard Children 2026: share where abuse or exploitation is suspected; seek consent where safe, but do not let lack of consent delay protection.

professional.t: Explain limits early, never promise secrecy, and tell her what you are doing and why unless that would put her or others at greater risk.
Document her words, the risk indicators, the discussion with the safeguarding lead, the referral and the plan. Follow up the referral outcome.

community.t: Children’s social care or the local multi-agency safeguarding hub; young people’s sexual-health services (for example Brook); pregnancy advice and abortion services; school nurse.

redFlags: Adult partner, secrecy, gifts, drugs or alcohol, control, or other young people involved — CSE indicators
Sex she did not want or could not refuse; pressure about the pregnancy decision
One-sided pain, bleeding or fainting — possible ectopic pregnancy
psychosocial: How the relationship started and how he treats her
Who she lives with, whether she feels safe, siblings, school
Who she could lean on; her emotional state
ice: Idea: “It’s a loving relationship — it’s not like that”
Concern: trouble for him and her family finding out; not knowing what to do
Expectation: private advice on options, no fuss

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “You’re pregnant, and you have real choices about what happens next. Because you’re 15 and your boyfriend is 22, I also have a duty to make sure you’re safe, and that means sharing this with the safeguarding team.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “The law sets an age of 16 to protect young people from relationships where the older person has more power — even when it feels loving. It’s about keeping you safe, not about blaming you.”

management.reflectIce: “You’re worried about him getting in trouble and your family finding out. I’ll be honest with you about every step, and I’ll help you through it — you won’t be on your own.”
management.psychosocial: Keep her trust: explain first, give her choices about contact, do not contact the partner, encourage (not force) a trusted adult, and keep pregnancy care moving.
sharedPlan: Same-day discussion with the safeguarding lead and referral to children’s social care
Non-directive options; prompt appointment with the pregnancy advice or abortion service; Gillick competence assessed
STI testing and contraception when she is ready
safetyNet: One-sided pain, heavy bleeding or fainting — A&E or 999; 999 if in danger
Phone call the next day; safe mobile contact agreed

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station fails candidates in two opposite directions: those who keep the secret to keep her happy, and those who deliver child-protection process so bluntly that a frightened 15-year-old disengages. The marks are in doing both jobs.

items.fail: Agreeing to keep it between you, or accepting “it’s not like that” and making no referral.
items.why: A 22-year-old with a 15-year-old is a child-protection concern that should be shared (Sexual Offences Act 2003 s9; GMC 0–18 years; Working Together 2026).
items.fix: Explain limits early and refer the same day through the safeguarding lead.

items.fail: Leading with “this is a crime and I must report him”.
items.why: She defends him, stops talking, and may not return — the risk is then unmanaged.
items.fix: Frame the duty around her safety: “It isn’t to punish you — it’s so you’re safe and supported.”

items.fail: Promising confidentiality at the start, then breaking it later.
items.why: “Did not explain the limits of confidentiality” — and it breaks trust at the moment she needs it most.
items.fix: State the limit before she tells you more, and tell her before you share.

items.fail: Focusing on safeguarding and forgetting the pregnancy.
items.why: Options are time-critical; delay removes choices. “Management plan insufficiently developed.”
items.fix: Give non-directive options and book the pregnancy-service appointment in the same consultation.

items.fail: Saying she needs a parent’s permission, or applying the Fraser guidelines to abortion.
items.why: Gillick competence applies to her decision about the pregnancy; Fraser is for contraception advice.
items.fix: Assess understanding and tell her she can decide if she understands; encourage a trusted adult.

items.fail: No safe contact plan, or contacting the boyfriend to “hear his side”.
items.why: Alerting a possible abuser can increase risk and hinder investigation.
items.fix: Agree a safe number, never contact the partner, and call her the next day.
